3.text: In another story collected in the same country, and also dealing with an

4.text: incident of real life, a man was killed by a neighbor. The body was cut in

5.text: pieces, and these were buried one by one in separate places. The family of

6.text: the victim thought he was lost somewhere in the country around. In order

7.text: to find him, they performed an incantation upon a dog, which was then

8.text: sent on the search. The dog found all the pieces one by one, and brought

9.text: them to the camp. They were put together by the relatives and burned on

10.text: the funeral pyre. After that the dog was killed in sacrifice to the World

11.text: (Ñaˊrgɪnên).² Then the family found the murderer and killed him. I have

12.text: mentioned also the important rôle of the dog in frightening away the “spirits

14.text: Incantation No. 9, c, which also was given to me as having a special

15.text: power to bring back the dead, is one of the usual incantations of magic

16.text: medicine. It calls down the Pebbly River, and then proclaims that the patient

17.text: is transformed into the rapid of its stream, and thus cleansed of all rubbish,

19.text: The love-incantations are of the usual symbolical type. In one (No. 11, a)

20.text: the performer watches the woman in question as she passes water, and then

21.text: pretends that the heart and intestines of the woman fall down together with

22.text: the water. After that he demands ice-creepers from the Morning-Dawn, and

23.text: tramples with them on the intestines of his victim.

24.text: In another incantation (No. 11, b) the performer proclaims that he is

25.text: about to extract the internal organs of the woman, whom he pretends to

26.text: entangle in a seal-net. Then he pretends to turn the husband of the woman

27.text: into a seal’s carcass, and the woman into a doe, which flees from the offensive

29.text: In still another incantation (No. 12) a jealous woman pretends to turn

30.text: her rival into carrion. She transforms the man in question into a big bear,

31.text: which eats of the carrion, but soon vomits it up.

32.text: It may be seen that, though the incantations were collected in different

33.text: and often quite distant localities, the methods used in them are similar even

35.text: The so-called “Raven Incantation” (No. 13) stands apart from the other

36.text: specimens of the kind. It was said to be used by shamans in order to

37.text: acquire power to harm other people. It is, however, only a dramatized form

38.text: of a tale well known to the Chukchee and to the Eskimo, both on the

39.text: Asiatic shore and in Alaska.⁴ It may be compared also with the actions of

40.text: mischievous shamans when they come out in the night-time and ask the su-

41.text: pernatural forces to give them power to harm their enemies.
